subtopic: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: Alpha Particle Deflection
question: A positively charged particle (alpha particle) projected toward the West is deflected toward the North by a magnetic field. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
options: Towards the South
Towards the East
Downwards into the page
Upwards (out of the page)
explanation: Since the alpha particle has a positive charge, the direction of current is along its motion (West). The deflection force is towards the North. Applying Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: align middle finger (current) to West, thumb (force) to North. The forefinger (magnetic field) points vertically upwards (out of the page).
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, NCERT In-Text Question Section 12.3

subtopic: Electron Deflection in Magnetic Field
question: An electron moves vertically downwards into a horizontal magnetic field directed towards the East. In which direction is the mechanical force acting on the electron directed?
options: Towards the North
Vertically upwards
Towards the South
Towards the West
explanation: Electrons carry negative charge, so the direction of conventional current is OPPOSITE to electron movement: electron moves downwards, so current is directed vertically upwards. Applying Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: Forefinger points East, Middle finger points upwards; the thumb points toward the South.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.3 Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

subtopic: Circular Coil: Multi-Turn Field Scaling
question: A circular coil of wire having N tightly wound turns carries an electric current I. How does the magnetic field produced at its center compare to that produced by a single turn of the same radius carrying the same current?
options: It is N times as large as that produced by a single turn
It is 1/N of the single turn field
It is N^2 times as large
It is identical to the single turn field because fields cancel
explanation: This is because the current in each circular turn has the exact same direction. As a result, the magnetic fields produced by the individual turns add up constructively (B_total = N * B_single).
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.2.2 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Circular Loop

subtopic: Straight Wire: Field vs Radial Distance
question: How does the magnitude of the magnetic field (B) at a point vary with perpendicular distance (r) from a long straight current-carrying wire?
options: Directly proportional to distance (B proportional to r)
Inversely proportional to distance (B proportional to 1/r)
Inversely proportional to square of distance (B proportional to 1/r^2)
Independent of distance r
explanation: The strength of the magnetic field produced by a straight wire is directly proportional to current (B proportional to I) and inversely proportional to radial distance (B proportional to 1/r). As one moves farther away, the concentric field lines become wider apart, indicating weakening field.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.2.1 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Straight Conductor

subtopic: Power Transmission: AC vs DC Long-Distance Advantage
question: What is the primary technical advantage of Alternating Current (AC) over Direct Current (DC) in national electrical grids?
options: AC is completely safe to touch without shock
AC generates zero heat in household appliances
AC circuits do not require switches or fuses
Electric power can be stepped up to extraordinarily high voltages by transformers and transmitted over long distances with minimal transmission losses
explanation: An important advantage of AC over DC is that electric power can be transmitted over very long distances without much loss of energy by stepping up the voltage with high-efficiency transformers, dramatically reducing line current and I^2*R transmission line heating.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.7 Domestic Electric Circuits

subtopic: Electromagnetic Induction: Discovery by Faraday
question: Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831. What is the fundamental principle of electromagnetic induction?
options: Relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field changes the magnetic flux linked with the conductor, inducing an electric current in it
A permanent magnet dissolves when exposed to alternating current
Electrons generate nuclear fission when passed through a solenoid
Electrostatic charges attract iron filings
explanation: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon of generating an induced electric current in a closed circuit by changing the magnetic field lines (magnetic flux) linked with the circuit, such as by moving a magnet relative to a coil.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.5 Electromagnetic Induction

subtopic: Induced Current: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule
question: Which rule is specifically applied to determine the direction of the INDUCED electric current in a moving conductor within a magnetic field?
options: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
Fleming's Right-Hand Rule
Maxwell's Corkscrew Rule
Ampere's Swimming Rule
explanation: Fleming's Right-Hand Rule determines the direction of induced current: stretch thumb (motion of conductor), forefinger (magnetic field), and middle finger (direction of induced current) mutually at right angles.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.5 Electromagnetic Induction

subtopic: Circuit Instruments: Galvanometer Role
question: What is the primary function of a Galvanometer in an electrical laboratory experiment?
options: To step down 220 V mains voltage
To convert AC into DC
To detect the presence and sense the direction of even tiny electric currents in a circuit
To measure electrical resistance directly in megaohms
explanation: A galvanometer is a sensitive instrument that can detect the presence of current in a circuit. Its pointer remains at zero (the center of the scale) for zero current. Depending on the direction of current, the pointer deflects either to the left or to the right.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.5 Electromagnetic Induction

subtopic: Fuse Placement: Mandatory Live Wire Installation
question: Why must an electric fuse ALWAYS be connected in series with the LIVE wire and NEVER in the neutral wire?
options: The neutral wire carries no electric current at all
Fuses can only conduct positive electric charges
If connected in the neutral wire, when the fuse blows due to a fault, the appliance remains connected to the 220 V live wire, presenting a lethal shock risk to anyone touching it
The neutral wire operates at higher temperature than the live wire
explanation: If a fuse is installed in the neutral line and blows, the connection to ground through neutral is broken, but the appliance remains energized at 220 V live potential. Touching the metal chassis will cause current to pass through the human body to ground, causing lethal shock. Placing it in the live wire isolates the appliance completely upon blowing.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.7 Domestic Electric Circuits

subtopic: Plug Standards: Three-Pin vs Two-Pin Classification
question: Why do heavy appliances like electric geysers and refrigerators require a three-pin plug with a thicker top pin, while mobile chargers and plastic hair dryers use two-pin plugs?
options: Mobile chargers operate on 440 V
The third pin is only used to charge batteries
Two-pin plugs prevent high electricity bills
Metal-bodied appliances have exposed conducting frames requiring earthing for safety; plastic appliances are 'double insulated' and have no exposed metal parts to carry shock
explanation: Appliances with metallic enclosures must have the earth wire bonded to their chassis via the third (longer and thicker) earth pin. If internal insulation fails, leakage current shunts to earth safely. Plastic-cased ('double insulated') devices have non-conducting exteriors that cannot become live, so a two-pin plug suffices.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.7 Domestic Electric Circuits

subtopic: Force on Stationary vs Moving Charges
question: A stationary alpha particle (charge +2e, velocity v = 0) is placed inside an extremely powerful 10 Tesla uniform magnetic field. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the alpha particle?
options: Zero Newtons
20 Newtons
3.2 * 10^-18 Newtons
Infinite force
explanation: Magnetic force on a charged particle is given by Lorentz magnetic force F = q * v * B * sin(theta). A magnetic field only exerts force on MOVING charges (v > 0). Because the particle is stationary (v = 0), the magnetic force acting on it is strictly zero.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.3 Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

subtopic: Overhead Power Line: Magnetic Field Direction
question: A horizontal high-voltage transmission line carries a heavy direct current from East to West. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point situated directly BELOW the wire?
options: Towards the North
Towards the South
Towards the East
Towards the West
explanation: Apply the Right-Hand Thumb Rule: point the right thumb toward the West (direction of current). Below the wire, the curled fingers wrap and point toward the South (and above the wire, they point toward the North).
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Example 12.1

subtopic: Field Line Density: Measurement of Field Strength
question: In a magnetic field line diagram, how is the relative strength (magnitude) of the magnetic field visually indicated?
options: By the thickness and color of the ink
By the degree of closeness (crowding) of the field lines
By the length of the straight segments
By the number of arrowheads drawn on each line
explanation: The relative strength of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of closeness of the field lines. Where the field lines are crowded close together (such as near the poles of a magnet), the magnetic field is strongest; where they are spaced widely apart, the field is weak.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.1 Magnetic Field and Field Lines

subtopic: Freely Suspended Solenoid: Alignment in Earth's Field
question: A current-carrying solenoid is suspended freely by a thin thread so that it can rotate horizontally. How does it align itself when coming to rest?
options: It spins continuously without stopping
It aligns strictly along the East-West line
It points vertically toward the center of the Earth
It aligns itself in the geographic North-South direction, exactly like a suspended bar magnet
explanation: A current-carrying solenoid behaves identical to a cylindrical bar magnet, having a North magnetic pole at one end and a South magnetic pole at the other. When suspended freely, it aligns in the Earth's geographic North-South direction.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.2.3 Magnetic Field due to a Current in a Solenoid

subtopic: Biomagnetism & Medical Imaging: MRI Technology
question: Which medical imaging modality relies on the extremely weak magnetic fields naturally produced by neural ion currents inside the human body (especially the brain and heart)?
options: X-ray Radiography
Ultrasound Sonography
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
explanation: Nerve impulses travel along neurons as ionic currents, producing tiny endogenous magnetic fields in organs such as the heart and brain. In hospital MRI scans, these internal biological fields interact with external superconducting magnets to construct detailed, high-resolution diagnostic cross-sections.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.3.1 Magnetism in Medicine

subtopic: Permanent Magnet Alloys: Alnico and Ferrite
question: Which specialized alloy is typically chosen for the industrial manufacture of powerful permanent magnets (such as those in audio loudspeakers)?
options: Alnico (alloy of aluminum, nickel, cobalt, and iron)
Soft annealed iron
Brass (copper and zinc)
Solder (lead and tin)
explanation: Permanent magnets require materials with high retentivity and high coercivity so they do not lose their magnetism over time or under mechanical shocks. Special ferromagnetic alloys like Alnico (Aluminum-Nickel-Cobalt) and Carbon Steel are used.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.2.3 Electromagnet

subtopic: Overloading Triggers in Domestic Wiring
question: Which of the following events can trigger an dangerous electrical overloading condition in a residential installation?
options: Connecting multiple high-power electrical appliances to a single multiple-socket adapter
A sudden unpredicted surge in the utility supply voltage
Direct accidental physical contact between the live wire and neutral wire
All of the above
explanation: Overloading occurs when total current drawn exceeds circuit capacity. This can be caused by plugging too many appliances into one socket, an unexpected supply voltage surge, or when live and neutral wires touch directly (short circuit), causing an extreme current surge.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.7 Domestic Electric Circuits

subtopic: Neutral Points in Magnetic Fields
question: What is a 'Neutral Point' in a magnetic field mapping experiment?
options: A point where a compass needle spins rapidly at 1000 rpm
A point where the magnetic field of the bar magnet is exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field, making the resultant net field zero
A point located exactly at the geometric center of the bar magnet
A point where gravity cancels magnetic attraction
explanation: At a neutral point, the magnetic field produced by the magnet is completely balanced and canceled out by Earth's horizontal magnetic field (B_net = 0). A compass needle placed at a neutral point experiences no orienting magnetic torque and can point in any arbitrary direction.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.1 Magnetic Field and Field Lines

subtopic: Magnetic Field of Straight Wire: Field Reversal
question: If the direction of electric current in a vertical wire is reversed from downwards to upwards, what happens to the direction of the magnetic field lines encircling the wire?
options: The field lines disappear permanently
The field lines transform into straight radial spokes
The field strength increases tenfold
The direction of the circular field lines reverses (e.g. from clockwise to anticlockwise when viewed from above)
explanation: By the Right-Hand Thumb Rule, reversing the direction of current reverses the sense of circulation of the concentric magnetic field lines (from clockwise to anticlockwise as viewed from above).
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.2.1 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Straight Conductor

subtopic: AC vs DC Frequency in Electricity
question: What is the frequency of direct current (DC) supplied by a dry chemical cell or storage battery?
options: 0 Hz (zero cycles per second)
50 Hz
60 Hz
100 Hz
explanation: Direct current (DC) flows continuously in one direction with constant polarity; it does not oscillate or alternate. Therefore, its frequency of alternation is exactly 0 Hz.
citation: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 12, Section 12.7 Domestic Electric Circuits
